title: 8 Reasons Why Your Body Is So Gross
summary: Josh and Chuck run through gross facts about the human body: demodex eyelash mites (and a fast mite, Paratarsotomus macropalpis, reported as the fastest land animal relative to size), earwax and ear candling, lipomas (fatty deposits), mucus production and boogers, flatulence and burping, vomiting and the chemoreceptor trigger zone, tonsil stones, and stomach acid protected by stomach mucus. The episode opens with banter about TV shows and closes with listener mail from Wendy of Good Good Girl praising the burlesque episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and TV talk
segments.summary: The hosts chat about The Wire, Oz, and haircuts, then set up the episode theme of gross things inside the human body.

segments.title: Demodex eyelash mites
segments.summary: Demodex mites live in hair follicles and pores on human faces, more common with age because of oil production. They move slowly at night and are generally harmless. Discussion of a fast mite species reported as the fastest land animal relative to body length.
topics: fastest land animal relative to size

segments.title: Earwax and ear candling
segments.summary: Earwax is self-cleaning and cotton swabs can push it deeper, causing impaction. Ear candles do not create a vacuum or remove wax and are a false claim. Mineral oil can soften hardened wax.

segments.title: Bloody noses and childhood ear aches
segments.summary: The hosts reminisce about childhood ear aches treated with warm oil and bloody noses, and note they may look into bloody noses later.

segments.title: Lipomas
segments.summary: Lipomas are benign fatty lumps between skin and muscle, usually painless and soft. They do not go away on their own. Options are liposuction or surgical removal; the hosts warn against self-removal.

segments.title: Mucus, snot, and boogers
segments.summary: The body produces about a quarter to half a gallon of mucus a day, which lubricates and protects tissues such as the stomach. Green mucus signals white blood cells fighting infection. Boogers are dried mucus, and the hosts discuss why kids eat them and the risks of nose picking.

segments.title: Burping and flatulence
segments.summary: Everyone burps and farts, roughly fourteen to twenty-three times a day combined. Gas comes from bacterial breakdown of food and swallowed air, and pressure changes on airplanes make people gassier. Gas contains methane, and flatulence is flammable.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short sponsor message between segments.

segments.title: Vomiting and the chemoreceptor trigger zone
segments.summary: The average stomach holds about three quarters of a gallon, and stomach rupture from overeating is rare. Vomiting is triggered by the chemoreceptor trigger zone, which receives signals from the vagus nerve and elsewhere, including the inner ear. The process involves salivation, retching, and pressure changes. The hosts discuss disgust as a nausea trigger and vomiting as a movie trope.

segments.title: Tonsil stones
segments.summary: Tonsil stones (tonsilloliths) form in tonsil pockets and can cause bad breath and other symptoms. Home remedies include tonsil irrigation, tongue brushing, and non-alcohol mouthwash; removal of tonsils is an option for chronic cases.

segments.title: Stomach acid
segments.summary: Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, kept from digesting the stomach by its mucus lining. Bile and acid from vomiting burn because there is less protective mucus in the throat and esophagus. Bulimia can damage teeth and raise rupture risk.

segments.title: Listener mail: high five from a feminist
segments.summary: Wendy Cyprit, editor of Good Good Girl, praises the burlesque episode and how the hosts handled feminist perspectives. The hosts thank her and give contact information.
